prompt.context: A company has an existing glass plant with a very high scrap rate — the yield is only 30% (scrap rate is 70%). The company is planning to build a new plant to meet anticipated demand.
prompt.question: Should the company use the existing technology from the old plant in the new plant, or should they implement a new (currently non-implemented at full scale) technology in the new plant?

clarifying_info.q: Can we improve the existing plant's yield?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. If you work on the process in the old plant, you can get the yield up to 50%. However, this improvement still will not meet anticipated demand — you will still need to build a new plant.

clarifying_info.q: If we build the new plant with old technology (at 50% yield), will that be enough capacity?
clarifying_info.a: The two plants combined (old improved + new with old tech) will meet current demand. If demand increases, you will have to build a third plant.

clarifying_info.q: Is the cost of the new facility different depending on which technology is chosen?
clarifying_info.a: No. The cost of the new facility is the same regardless of the technology chosen. However, the plant cannot be retooled from one technology to another without a significant investment.

clarifying_info.q: Are there differences in fixed or overhead costs between the two technologies?
clarifying_info.a: No significant difference in fixed or overhead costs associated with the two technologies.

clarifying_info.q: Has the new technology been proven at scale?
clarifying_info.a: The new technology is currently being run on a small-scale basis only. The company is running it successfully on a small scale but is worried that it has not been tested in a full-scale production environment.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a difference in customer preference or pricing between the two technologies?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Customers prefer the product manufactured with the new technology and will pay a price premium for it. Since no other companies have this technology, the company could increase market share if the new technology is chosen.

framework: Establish whether a new plant is truly necessary: analyze demand vs. current capacity, potential improvements to existing facilities, and alternatives such as outsourcing
Frame the decision as a comparison of two alternatives using cash flows and NPV
Evaluate benefits of the new technology: price premium, increased market share, higher capacity (no third plant needed), competitive differentiation
Evaluate risks of the new technology: unproven at full production scale, no ability to retool if it fails
Weigh strategic fit: long-term demand outlook, competitive landscape, and capital commitment

questions.prompt: Is it truly necessary to build a new plant?
questions.guidance: Candidate should probe current capacity utilization, demand forecasts, and alternatives. The case confirms a new plant is necessary — the old plant at 50% yield plus any improvements still cannot meet anticipated demand. Outsourcing and other alternatives have been ruled out.

questions.prompt: Compare the NPV of the two technology options.
questions.guidance: Candidate should request financial data (revenues, costs, volumes, discount rate) and structure the comparison. Key NPV drivers: (1) Old technology — lower revenue per unit (no price premium), combined two-plant capacity only meets current demand, a third plant would be needed if demand grows; (2) New technology — price premium on all units, higher market share, two plants sufficient even if demand grows, but execution risk if scale-up fails. Without specific numbers provided, candidate should articulate the framework: NPV = PV of incremental revenues (price premium × volume) minus PV of any incremental costs or risk-adjusted losses.

math.setup: No specific numerical data given in the case. Framework: NPV(new tech) = PV(price premium × volume) + PV(market share gains) - PV(risk-adjusted cost of scale-up failure). NPV(old tech) = baseline, but requires a third plant if demand grows, adding future capex.
steps: Estimate incremental revenue from price premium under new technology
Estimate avoided future capex (no third plant) under new technology
Risk-adjust for probability of scale-up failure
math.answer: Decision depends on magnitude of price premium, demand growth probability, and assessed risk of new technology failing at scale. Qualitatively, new technology has a stronger NPV if the price premium and market share gains are meaningful and scale-up risk is manageable.

questions.prompt: What are the key risks of choosing the new technology, and how would you mitigate them?
questions.guidance: Main risk is that the new technology is unproven at full production scale. Mitigation options: phased rollout, parallel running of old technology as backup, negotiating performance guarantees with technology vendor, building contingency capital into the plan. Candidate should also note that if the new plant fails to operate, the company is locked in (retooling is a significant investment).

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the potential benefits of choosing the new technology for the new plant?

categories.name: Revenue upside
ideas: Price premium from customers who prefer the new-technology product
Increased market share since no competitors have the technology
Higher volume potential without needing a third plant

categories.name: Cost and capacity
ideas: No future capex for a third plant if demand grows
Two plants sufficient to meet growing demand at higher yield

categories.name: Strategic / competitive
ideas: Barrier to entry for competitors who lack the technology

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Potentially lower per-unit production cost over time

recommendation: Recommend building the new plant with the new technology, provided the company can adequately manage scale-up risk
The new technology offers a price premium, market share gains, and avoids the need for a costly third plant — all of which improve long-term NPV relative to the old technology
risks: New technology is unproven at full production scale — if it fails, the company faces significant losses and cannot retool cheaply
Capital is locked into the technology choice; a bad outcome is difficult and expensive to reverse
next_steps: Commission a detailed technical assessment and pilot to stress-test the new technology at near-full scale before final commitment
Model the NPV under multiple scenarios (base, downside scale-up failure, upside high demand growth) to quantify the risk-return tradeoff
Negotiate risk-sharing arrangements (warranties, performance guarantees) with the technology provider
Ensure the old plant's yield improvement to 50% is implemented as a bridge to maintain supply during new plant construction
